entries.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Alex Bregman win Gold Glove Awards, backing Cubs' reputation as baseball's best defense
entries.summary: <p>The Cubs had baseball’s best defense in 2026, and it wasn’t even close.</p><p>Now, they’ve got the hardware to prove it.</p><p>Center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong and third baseman Alex Bregman won Gold Gloves when the annual position-by-position defensive awards were announced Sunday night.</p><p>Three other Cubs – shortstop Dansby Swanson, left fielder Ian Happ and right fielder Seiya Suzuki – were previously announced as finalists at their respective positions but did not win.</p><p>Still, between the winners and the near-winners, the team’s reputation as the sport’s finest in the field was backed up in a big way.</p><p>The statistics did that plenty prior to Sunday’s haul, with the Cubs boasting massive leads in defensive metrics like Outs Above Average (73, compared to the 44 of the second-place Diamondbacks), Defensive Runs Saved (115, compared to the 87 of the second-place Rays) and Fielding Run Value (72, compared to the 46 mark of the second-place Blue Jays).</p><p>So whether you prefer numbers or trophies, there was no question: The Cubs were baseball’s best defensive team.</p><p>The eye test, if that’s your thing, did a lot to seal that argument, too, and the Cubs spent the summer making one fantastic play after another, talking often about defense as the backbone of a team built to contend for a championship.</p><p>That championship, of course, never came, and as good as the gloves were, they did little to stave off postseason embarrassment. The Cubs stumbled in the regular season’s final week, failing to secure home-field advantage in the wild-card round, and were swept without putting up too much fight in just two games against the Padres.</p><p>That finish might dominate the memory of fans, but they watched an otherwise thrilling summer at Wrigley Field – and the defense had a lot to do with that.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong, who’s expected to win the NL MVP, made defense a cornerstone of his case for the sport’s top individual award, with his excellence in the field and at the plate compared to the two-way dominance of Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani, creating a meaty debate prior to late-season health issues that took Ohtani out of the race.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong’s defensive exploits helped him to a jaw-dropping 10.6 fWAR that dwarfed that of all other position players in the game. This Gold Glove was his second in as many seasons.</p><p>Bregman, now a two-time Gold Glover, isn’t going anywhere after the Cubs locked him up last offseason, and that’s great news for them after the 32-year-old posted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/05/cubs-alex-bregman-defense-gold-glove-ryan-zeferjahn-save-javier-assad-marlins" >perhaps the best defensive season of his career</a> at the hot corner. His 15 Defensive Runs Saved nearly doubled his previous career high, and he set a new career high with eight Outs Above Average, as well.</p><p>Bregman became the Cubs’ first Gold Glover at third base since Ron Santo in 1968.</p>

entries.title: PHOTOS: Little Village celebrates Día de los Muertos
entries.summary: <p>Little Village's 26th Street transformed into a mass celebration for Día de los Muertos on Sunday. </p><p>The holiday, which means Day of the Dead in English, is an annual tradition on Nov. 1 and 2 in Mexico and Central Latin American countries to honor and celebrate loved ones who have died. People decorate ofrendas (altars in English) with marigolds, sugar skulls and photos of their loved ones. </p><p>On Saturday and Sunday, dozens of Little Village businesses — including bakeries, taquerías, flower shops, boutiques, banks and cultural spaces — joined in on the celebration hosted by the Little Village Chamber of Commerce. Participating businesses made ofrendas and staff dressed up as catrines and catrinas. </p><p>Check out all the festivities: </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Caleb Williams for MVP? Monday is a prime time to state his case
entries.summary: <p>Whether Caleb Williams gives himself a chance to win NFL MVP or not, it won’t be for lack of exposure.</p><p>If he were in the running for the Heisman Trophy, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears’</a> primetime broadcast run between now and Christmas would be a point in his favor. If the quarterback was running for Senate, national television games would be his big end-of-cycle ad buy.</p><p>Monday night’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/31/bears-report-te-colston-loveland-good-to-go-vs-seahawks-despite-neck-injury" target="_blank" >game in Seattle</a>, then, figures to chart the course for the next two months of Williams discourse. He’s got the seventh-best odds to win the MVP, at 22-1, despite missing three games due to injury. But he has plenty of prominent opportunities — against some of the NFL’s best teams — to state his case.</p><p>“You have to hold yourself to a certain standard,” Williams said. “And that's what these primetime games are — they're the league seeing us as one of those teams that's the best in football.”</p><p>The Bears improved to 5-2 with a primetime win against the Patriots. They’ll follow their “Monday Night Football” game with a “Sunday Night Football” matchup against the Buccaneers at Soldier Field.On Thanksgiving, he’ll play a standalone game against the Lions. On Dec. 19, the Bears will play a primetime Saturday night game in Buffalo. Their rivalry game against the Packers at noon Christmas Day will be the only game in its time slot, too. That list doesn’t include any possible flexed-game scenarios, either — if the Bears remain one of the hottest teams in football, they could play even more night games.</p><p>“We want to go out there and prove ourselves each and every week — it doesn't matter if it's primetime or not,” Williams said. “But in that sense of it being primetime, that's what the league wants for us. That's what we want for ourselves.”</p><p>When the Bears traded for four-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons this week — and the Seahawks for eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson — Monday night’s game became, for some, a preview of the NFC championship. It will also be another national referendum on Williams and his chances to be considered among the best players — at any position — in the NFL.</p><p>“This isn't a rival game for us, but it's a big game,” Williams said. “It's on primetime. They're going to be loud. They're the reigning champs, and so I'm excited for it.”</p><p>He has every reason to be. Williams is trending the way the Bears have always dreamed, posting a completion percentage above coach Ben Johnson’s stated goal of 70% and throwing only one interception in four games. He posted a passer rating of 111.2 against the Falcons and 116.7 against the Patriots after returning from a hamstring injury. Johnson thought he could have been better against the Patriots, though — and the quarterback agreed.</p><p>“I love just where he is, mindset-wise, right now,” Johnson said. “No one's more critical of him than himself at this point. And as good as he's done taking care of the football — and certainly the higher completion percentage and all those things — we would come in, and there's a lot more to be had last week.”</p><p>Williams’ performances encouraged general manager Ryan Poles to trade two first-round picks as part of a package for Simmons as part of the Bears’ Super Bowl push.</p><p>“A lot of hope and belief in our quarterback — and the path that he's on,” Poles said.</p><p>It’s been since the Bears’ last Super Bowl appearance, probably, that the Bears were considered such a serious contender to win a championship. The monoliths that stood in front of them last year — the Rams and Seahawks — aren’t running away with the NFC as the season comes close to its halfway point.</p><p>Monday night, then, will be a measuring stick.</p><p>“We've been saying all week long that we're gonna have to coach the best that we've coached all year, we're gonna have to play the best that we've played all year,” Johnson said. “And that doesn't mean we're scared to make mistakes or anything like that, but we got to be on our mess. We can't shoot ourselves in the foot with turnovers or penalties or things of that nature. ….</p><p>“It'll be a great tape to look at, just to assess where we are.”</p><p>And where Williams is. Last week, the Seahawks bullied Patrick Mahomes into the worst game of his illustrious career. The Chiefs scored just three points and didn’t post a pass of at least 20 yards or a run of at least 10. None of that had ever happened with Mahomes under center.</p><p>When Williams walks to the line of scrimmage Monday, the Seahawks will be in a shell with two high safeties. Their coverage, though, will morph depending on what the Bears do immediately after the snap. If the Bears send a running back into the flat quickly, for example, a safety could cover him. If the release is slow, though, the safety would go elsewhere.</p><p>“You may not know what the coverage is at any given time or where the pressure's coming from at any given time,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. “And we try to build in this standard operating procedure of how we're going to respond to any of it — and all of it — and make sure we're putting our guys in the best position.”</p><p>Williams needs to know the rules of the defense, then, and play with enough anticipation to attack it. That’s a tough ask.</p><p>Master it, though, and Williams could start stating his MVP case.</p>

entries.title: Bears' defense rebuilding on the fly as Jeffery Simmons arrives, Kyler Gordon revs up, Montez Sweat returns
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive coordinator Dennis Allen usually seems annoyed by having to do a weekly news conference, but coming off <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/31/jeffery-simmons-trade-bears-gm-ryan-poles-pursues-legendary-stuff-as-super-bowl-chase-officially-begins" >the trade for star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons</a>, talking to the media didn’t bother him at all.</p><p>Normally ultra-serious, Allen bordered on wacky as he cartoonishly looked side to side when two reporters asked him a question at the same time and he flashed a big smile as he said he felt like he was in the middle of a ping-pong match.</p><p>Simmons was quite a mood lifter for a defense that already was feeling better and better about itself heading toward the Bears’ visit to the defending champion Seahawks on Monday.</p><p>Allen’s job just became more fun. Defensive line has been a weak spot for years — imagine how Matt Eberflus must’ve reacted to general manager Ryan Poles acquiring an All-Pro defensive tackle — and Allen has constantly had to scheme around that and other deficiencies over his first season and a half.</p><p>That won’t be quite as necessary anymore.</p><p>“You get a guy like this and it frees up a lot of things,” coach Ben Johnson said. “It takes a lot of shortcomings and can mask those to a degree. When you’ve got a defensive player that’s as dominant as this guy is, it just takes him making a play to cover up some things across the board.</p><p>“He’s going to elevate everybody around him. Just having him out there is going to do wonders.”</p><p>The Bears got livewire nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon back from an injury two weeks ago. Then they added Simmons. Defensive end Montez Sweat returns Monday from a two-game suspension. Pieces are clicking into place, and the defense is being rebuilt on the fly.</p><p>It’s good timing as they go up against the Seahawks.</p><p>As hot as quarterback Caleb Williams and the offense have been, it’s brutally tough to score on these guys. Patrick Mahomes walked out of Lumen Field last week with three points.</p><p>They led the NFL in fewest points allowed last season at 17.2 per game and are fourth this season at 17.9.</p><p>To give themselves a chance, the Bears must contain a Seahawks offense stocked with dangerous pieces.</p><p>Wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba is chasing the first 2,000-yard season in league history. At running back, Zach Charbonnet was integral to their championship run, and rookie Jadarian Price is a first-round pick. Sam Darnold has struggled, but made the Pro Bowl the last two seasons and can’t be counted out.</p><p>But the upside for the Bears is they’ll need less smoke and mirrors to deal with all that. Simmons’ arrival should lead to more one-on-one matchups for everyone else on the defensive line, and the faster that group pushes into the backfield, the easier gets for everyone behind it.</p><p>And suddenly the Bears’ defense would look closer to what’s required to take a shot at the Super Bowl.</p><p>“We’re adding people and we’re getting there,” Gordon said. “It is nice to feel complete and complement each other in the ways that we all want to. We’re going to do a lot of great things.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs' Mike Montgomery had the all-time moment in 2016. After that? Baseball wasn't easy
entries.summary: <p>Mike Montgomery got the call. Then he got the ground ball.</p><p>A man could live 1,000 baseball lives and never come through in a bigger moment than two outs in the 10th inning of Game 7 of the 2016 World Series in Cleveland.</p><p>Throughout Cubdom, Montgomery’s one-out save — the first of his professional career — will live forever. Ten years since Nov. 2, 2016, the 37-year-old still can close his eyes and feel the rush of it.</p><p>“The highest high imaginable,” he says.</p><p>How many pitchers can say they got a final out that endures as toweringly as that one? But baseball isn’t a storybook, and Montgomery had to fight with all his might for every inch of success in the game after the night to end all nights. A former Royals first-round pick who threw back-to-back shutouts in his first month in the majors with the Mariners in 2015, Montgomery still believed after being traded to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> in July of 2016 that he could become “one of the best players ever in the game.” Needless to say, that didn’t happen.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/HOp8w2PgHlM?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Cubs win World Series with Game 7 win"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Instead, a lefty whom Kyle Hendricks predicted the following spring would become the Cubs’ next pitching star lasted another two-plus seasons on the North Side — never truly locking down a rotation spot — and was dealt in 2019 back to the Royals, with whom he fizzled out. From there, it was an odyssey: Montgomery was released in spring training by the Mets, bombed out in the minors with the Yankees, had an unsuccessful stint in Korea, gave it another go with the Mets in Triple-A but got shelled, signed with a Mexican League team but was soon released, pitched forgettably in the Dodgers’ system and in 2024 — making less than $3,000 a month in one last gasp — turned out to be just another arm for the Long Island Ducks of the independent Atlantic League.</p><p>It was over.</p><p>No more storybook moments. No more dream.</p><p>Fortunately, no regrets the size of which keep a man up at night.</p><p>“I’ve been in the highest of highs and then been in Mexico sitting there sick from the water, thinking, ‘What am I doing? I’ve got a two-year-old and a daughter about to be born.’ In Long Island, here I am a World Series champ with six years in the big leagues. I was throwing 90, 92, thought my stuff was good enough, but nobody called. …</p><p>“But I’ve talked with some close friends and my wife about this: What if I would’ve had a 12-year career and made hundreds of millions but never won anything? To be a part of one of the best moments in baseball history, I don’t think there’s enough money for that. I wouldn’t trade it for anything. It’s not like we’re broke. I could’ve had a better career, made more, but I had the kind of pinnacle moment that I can take with me forever.”</p><p>Since May, Montgomery, who lives in Scottsdale, Arizona, with his family, has been the rehab pitching coach for the Mariners, a job he’s enjoying. Son Max and daughter Zoe are growing. Life is good. Any regrets are small enough.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e00000" not where I want to be considering I’ve already been to the top of the mountain,’ ” he says. “I’ve had to work through that, but I’m at peace with it. I’m very proud of my career. Man, I wish I could have been a 10-, 15-year player, All-Star games, all that. I may not have been the best player to ever play, but I have been to the best moment in baseball history.”</p><p>Among his worst moments: being ejected from a 2021 game in Korea with the Samsung Lions, and suspended for three weeks, having gone after a “disrespectful” umpire and needed to be held back by several teammates before pelting the ump with a rosin bag.</p><p>Nobody’s perfect.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/10/30/2016-cubs-world-series-chicago-jake-arrieta-jon-lester-ben-zobrist-dexter-fowler-cleveland-mlb" target="_blank" >2016 Cubs roundtable: World Series stars take fresh look back at just how good team really was</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Montgomery was far from perfect after going from Seattle’s rotation to the Cubs’ bullpen just before the 2016 trade deadline. He met the Cubs in Milwaukee, where he gave up a homer in his first appearance. In his next appearance, he got walked off by the White Sox. By the time he got to his locker at Wrigley Field for the first time, a letter from a “fan” was waiting for him.</p><p>“You’re the worst player ever. You must be pitching with the wrong arm,” Montgomery remembers it saying.</p><p>Not long after the final out in Cleveland, Montgomery actually wrote that person back — the only fan letter he ever returned. The message spanned all of seven words:</p><p>“I hope you enjoyed the World Series.”</p><p>Signed, Mike Montgomery.</p><p>That, too, would be mighty damn hard for anyone to top.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/n74vh2xJFOI?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="KBO Ejection - Former MLB Pitcher Mike Montgomery Throws Rosin Bag at Umpire After Warning for Delay"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Readers call for action to protect neglected senior
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR READERS:</b> The mailbox was bursting with responses to the Oct. 9 letter from Frustrated Neighbor, whose 94-year-old neighbor is bedridden and nominally cared for by a woman who also holds his power of attorney. I'll let the readers speak for themselves:</p><p>"Red flags everywhere! The neighbor says the caregiver has his POA, which means she can control his money. She has no incentive to move him to a home. A person who is 100% bedridden shouldn't be alone for 18 hours each day. This is elder abuse in my mind and quite possibly fraud. One phone call is all it should take if she explains the situation." — <i>RED FLAGS</i></p><p>"The person who wrote in should contact Adult Protective Services to make sure an unbiased individual looks at the situation and does what is necessary and what the elderly person wants. I am an attorney and volunteer member of our county's Adult Protective Service Multidisciplinary Team. We see this sort of situation all the time." — <i>ON WATCH</i></p><p>"The poor bedbound man is a victim of abuse and neglect, and the situation should be reported to the authorities immediately. If he's regularly being ignored for 18 hours or more, I'm sure he has bedsores or worse." — <i>UNNERVED</i></p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Alzheimer's disease affects millions of Americans and their families, and the need for new approaches to treatment remains urgent. As a physician in the Division of Geriatrics at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), I've seen how deeply this disease can affect not only people living with Alzheimer's, but also the families and caregivers who support them. Today, I'm encouraged by the opportunity to help identify new approaches to treating Alzheimer's disease as the principal investigator at a new clinical trials site in Oakland, California. One of our goals is to make clinical research more accessible and to increase participation among communities that historically have been underrepresented in clinical trials.</p><p>Abby, clinical trials cannot succeed without volunteers. Just as importantly, the people who participate in research should reflect the diverse communities affected by Alzheimer's disease. By broadening participation, we hope to learn more about potential treatments while helping ensure that advances in Alzheimer's research can benefit everyone.</p><p>At our site, we are currently enrolling participants in the SPRING Trial, a clinical study for people ages 55 to 80 who have been diagnosed with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease. SPRING is exploring a different approach to Alzheimer's treatment: targeting P. gingivalis, a bacterium associated with gum disease that can also make its way into our brains. The drug LHP588 is designed to inactivate toxic enzymes produced by this bacterium, with the goal of stopping or slowing down the progression of Alzheimer's disease.</p><p>I hope your readers who are living with Alzheimer's disease, or caring for someone who is, will consider learning more about the SPRING Trial and whether participation might be right for them. More information about the study and participating sites across the U.S. can be found at springclinicaltrial.com. — <i>T. RICHARD PARENTEAU, M.D./PH.D. PRINCIPAL INVESTIGATOR, OAKLAND CLINICAL RESEARCH VOLUNTEER CLINICAL PROFESSOR, UCSF DIVISION OF GERIATRICS</i></p><p><b>DEAR DR. PARENTEAU:</b> I'm happy to help spread the word that volunteers are needed for this important study. Readers, if someone you know might be a candidate for this trial, I urge you to visit the website!</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: Bears-Seahawks: What to watch for
entries.summary: <h3><b>WHEN THE BEARS HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p>Ben Johnson was impressed by Devon Witherspoon’s University of Illinois film long before he became the second-highest-paid cornerback in the NFL. In the last year-and-a-half, he’s seen him grow even more, as the Seahawks have moved him from the slot to outside cornerback.</p><p>The Bears coach said he “still finds a way to impact the game” despite not being around the ball as often as he was in the slot. The numbers support his hunch — Pro Football Focus gives him the 10<sup>th</sup>-best coverage grade of all NFL cornerbacks to play at least half their team’s snaps.</p><p>Safety Julian Love is second among safeties. He’s one of the most accomplished Chicago-area natives in the NFL, having won the Sun-Times’ Football Player of the Year Award in 2015 while playing for Nazareth Academy in La Grange Park. He attended Notre Dame before being drafted by the Giants. He recorded his first career interception in 2019 off Mitch Trubisky at Soldier Field and picked off Drake Maye in Super Bowl LX.</p><p>Up front, the Seahawks boast edge rusher DeMarcus Lawrence and defensive tackles Leonard Williams and Byron Murphy, all of whom rank in the top 20 in pass-rush win rate at their position.</p><p>The Seahawks rank second in the NFL in havoc rate, which measures how often a defense gets a sack, pressure, tackle for loss, forced fumble, interception or pass breakup. Since giving up 31 points to the Commanders in Week 3, the Seahawks have allowed 18 points per game — including just three against the Chiefs last week.</p><h3><b>WHEN THE SEAHAWKS HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p>The Bears and Seahawks each made blockbuster trades this week. Monday night, they’ll face off against each other, the same way they did Oct. 18 when guard Quenton Nelson still played for the Colts and Jeffery Simmons played defensive tackle for the Titans. The two had played in the same division since 2019; Nelson joked this week that he can’t find a way to get away from Simmons.</p><p>The Seahawks tried to shore up their offensive line by trading a third-round pick for Nelson, who’s made a Pro Bowl in all eight of his seasons. They’d struggled until the Chiefs game, giving up a combined 10 sacks and 26 quarterback hits in back-to-back losses to the 49ers and Broncos. Against Kansas City, they gave up no sacks and just two hits on Sam Darnold. The quarterback was sharp, posting a passer rating of 96.9 after having a 64.6 and 52.6 in the previous two weeks.</p><p>After letting Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker sign with the Chiefs in March, the Seahawks have struggled to get production at running back. Entering Week 8, only eight teams averaged fewer yards per carry than the Seahawks’ 3.9.</p><p>Veteran running back Zach Charbonnet, who tore his knee last year, will make his season debut Monday. First-round Jadarian Price hasn’t played since Week 4 because of a chest injury. He’s not carrying an injury designation, but the Seahawks need to activate the running back off injured reserve Monday afternoon in order to play.</p>

entries.title: Two-thirds of 2026 Taste of Chicago vendors flagged with health code violations
entries.summary: <p>Overflowing garbage. Backed-up sinks. Food prepped in bushes. More than 800 pounds of food tossed due to improper temperatures.</p><p>These are just a few examples of food safety problems city inspectors documented during one hot weekend in July when one of the city’s largest culinary events, Taste of Chicago, took place in Grant Park.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/07/08/taste-of-chicago-2026-international-best-dishes-information-bands-food-music?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23559714611&gbraid=0AAAAA9e-Tg5VxE5WxGiR1TbfeYoag_n7F&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhG9MZ_Um4PVpY0GynUiDfJ0OSHL87U1JaijlSabpWuLi-ANa1mGtPhoCMCcQAvD_BwE" target="_blank" ><u>food festival</u></a> kicked off as the country was still grappling with a Cyclospora outbreak that disrupted food systems and left consumers guessing what's safe to eat, all amid a rollback of federal regulations.</p><p>Chicago is a festival-friendly city, and after another jam-packed summer event season, WBEZ/Sun-Times wanted to know how Chicago inspects food at major outdoor events. We also wanted to know which events city sanitarians inspect — and found little evidence that some private events, like Lollapalooza, are inspected at all.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ec0000" name="image-ec0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/61b9b72/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fcf%2F59324cef4895989e747c3c808b1b%2Ftasteopens-090724-13.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a8d17b4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fcf%2F59324cef4895989e747c3c808b1b%2Ftasteopens-090724-13.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7de9ae3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fcf%2F59324cef4895989e747c3c808b1b%2Ftasteopens-090724-13.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The Taste of Chicago, pictured here in 2024, is a popular summer festival. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7de9ae3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fcf%2F59324cef4895989e747c3c808b1b%2Ftasteopens-090724-13.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aa214f2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fcf%2F59324cef4895989e747c3c808b1b%2Ftasteopens-090724-13.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7de9ae3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2Fcf%2F59324cef4895989e747c3c808b1b%2Ftasteopens-090724-13.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Taste of Chicago, pictured here in 2024, is a popular summer festival. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>At Taste of Chicago this year, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/07/08/taste-of-chicago-2026-international-best-dishes-information-bands-food-music" target="_blank" ><u>81 vendors</u></a> served up regional and international dishes to thousands of people across five days. According to records obtained by WBEZ/Sun-Times from the Chicago Department of Public Health and the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events, inspectors logged more than 160 health code violations during the festival. More than half of vendors listed received violations, our analysis shows.</p><p>Some on-site infractions were minor, like slow-draining sinks, employees in tank tops and missing food safety licenses. Others were far more troubling, like food being prepared in bushes and stored at unsafe temperatures in the summer heat.</p><p>The records also revealed a potential lack of oversight in the city’s application process. Local food vendors go through a lengthy approval process to participate in Taste of Chicago that includes submitting business certifications and a clean health inspection of a brick-and-mortar site or food truck within six months of the festival application date, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health and the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events.</p><p>But according to a WBEZ/Sun-Times analysis of records, including Taste application materials and restaurant inspections, fewer than half of the 81 vendors met those requirements.</p><p>All vendors serving food at Taste ultimately had a “pass” on file with the health department before the event, although many of those passed inspections were outdated and outside of the application’s required six-month window. According to records analyzed by WBEZ/Sun-Times, others only had a conditional pass on file. (Inspectors pass a restaurant with conditions when it has some violations but not enough to be an immediate hazard for food safety.)</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-880000" name="html-embed-module-880000"></a><div style="min-height:539px" id="datawrapper-vis-8sa4Y"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/8sa4Y/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-8sa4Y"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/8sa4Y/full.png" alt="Two thirds of vendors at Taste had at least one health code violation, and fewer than half had compliant applications (Small multiple donut chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>What’s more, nine restaurants failed inspections at their brick-and-mortar locations in the months between applying and the festival start date.</p><p>One example is Ponce Restaurant, at 4313 W. Fullerton Ave., which submitted an application on April 21, then failed an inspection on June 24 — just two weeks before Taste. One of the city’s health inspectors noted <a class="Link" href="https://data.cityofchicago.org/Health-Human-Services/Food-Inspections/4ijn-s7e5/explore/query/SELECT%0A%20%20%60inspection_id%60%2C%0A%20%20%60dba_name%60%2C%0A%20%20%60aka_name%60%2C%0A%20%20%60license_%60%2C%0A%20%20%60facility_type%60%2C%0A%20%20%60risk%60%2C%0A%20%20%60address%60%2C%0A%20%20%60city%60%2C%0A%20%20%60state%60%2C%0A%20%20%60zip%60%2C%0A%20%20%60inspection_date%60%2C%0A%20%20%60inspection_type%60%2C%0A%20%20%60results%60%2C%0A%20%20%60violations%60%2C%0A%20%20%60latitude%60%2C%0A%20%20%60longitude%60%2C%0A%20%20%60location%60%0AWHERE%20%60license_%60%20IN%20%28%222988888%22%29%0AORDER%20BY%20%60inspection_date%60%20DESC%20NULL%20FIRST/page/filter" target="_blank" ><u>“evidence of rodent activity on the premises,”</u></a> citing approximately 35 mouse droppings throughout the rear storage area and behind chest freezers and storage racks at the brick-and-mortar location. Inspectors also reported opened food packages stored without proper labels.</p><p>When Ponce was re-inspected on July 2, a week before the Taste festival, city inspectors passed the restaurant. The report doesn't indicate any issues regarding pests or pest control but didn’t note how the rodent droppings were addressed.</p><p>But at the Taste, records show inspectors failed Ponce for <a class="Link" href="https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28858265-ponce-toc2026-inspections/" target="_blank" ><u>three out of the vendor’s four inspections conducted on the first day</u></a>, including for holding food at improper temperatures. A few days later at the festival, the same issue prompted the restaurant to discard at least 95 pounds of pork, plantains, lettuce and tomatoes. Ponce Restaurant didn’t reply to several requests for comment.</p><p>It wasn’t just booths that had issues leading up to — or at — Taste. Food truck Yummy Halal failed a June 16 inspection, just 22 days before Taste, when a city inspector observed “approximately 40 or more rat droppings” on the floor of the business’ food truck, plus wastewater streaming from the exterior water tank onto a city street, according to a report.</p><p>Then, while at Taste, the food truck <a class="Link" href="https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28858267-yummyhalal-toc2026-inspections/" target="_blank" ><u>failed five health inspections</u></a>, with violations including improper holding temperatures of ingredients and a lack of hair restraints. The food truck was later shut down for the day by city inspectors for failing to have a certified manager on-site. Yummy Hall didn’t respond to requests for comment either.</p><p>While the Chicago Department of Public Health didn’t indicate any signs of foodborne illness as a result of 2026’s Taste, in 2007, the department <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2007/07/15/illnesses-reported-from-taste-triple-2/" target="_blank" ><u>inspected a Salmonella outbreak after the event</u></a> as a result of a hummus dish from vendor Pars Cove Persian Cuisine. The outbreak sickened more than 300 people.</p><p>Researchers have found that issues with temperature control tend to be the <a class="Link" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11908744/#sec16" target="_blank" ><u>leading contributors to foodborne illness outbreaks</u></a> involving bacteria such as Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria and Staph. And the foot traffic Taste can receive, combined with the hot temps, can mean that improperly stored food can put people at risk.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-070000" name="image-070000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Foodies walk around on the first day of Taste of Chicago 2026 in Grant Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Food in the hot sun </b></h3><p>WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times analyzed thousands of pages of records from the 2026 Taste of Chicago obtained from city agencies via the Freedom of Information Act. We built a database of each vendor and their health inspection data, both at the festival and at the restaurants’ year-round brick and mortar locations. We found:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-20359b12-d48c-11f1-83b4-7d53e9605cda"><li>Vendors failed a health inspection at Taste if city inspectors found one or more violations. According to records, 58 different vendors had at least one health code violation at Taste. But 10 vendors had five or more violations. Two vendors had nine.</li><li>Only 35 of the 81 vendors had health inspections in their applications that met city criteria — a “pass” within the past six months before applying for Taste.</li><li>The most common issues at Taste were temperature related: Inspectors identified 82 violations related to holding food at an incorrect temperature, and seven for faulty coolers and facilities, making up more than half of all violations issued at the festival.</li></ul><p>The latter list included Josephine’s Southern Cooking, which applied with an outdated health inspection. The restaurant ultimately passed an inspection between its application and the festival itself. But at Taste, it was cited for washing dishes and preparing food on site — two actions that are not allowed. On the last day of the festival, inspectors <a class="Link" href="https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28858266-josephines-toc2026-inspections/" target="_blank" ><u>failed the booth for filling shrimp dumplings on a folding table behind their tent</u></a> along hedges in the park.</p><p>Oooh Wee Smothered, a spin-off of Chatham staple Oooh We! It Is!, had a clean health inspection just a month and a half before they applied to Taste, fully in compliance with the city’s requirements.</p><p>But at the festival itself, the restaurant racked up <a class="Link" href="https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28858268-ooohwee-toc2026-inspections/" target="_blank" ><u>nine different violations across two days</u></a>. That included failing their first inspection for not having someone on site with a certificate, holding food at improper temperatures and storing cooked chicken in a container that previously contained raw chicken.</p><p>The certificate holder came back on site, and the food was discarded. But a few days later, Oooh Wee was cited for prepping food on site, a mayo-based sauce testing overly warm and a too-hot cooler.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-770000" name="module-770000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>WHAT WE DID TO REPORT THIS STORY</b><br><br>To look at how vendors at Taste of Chicago were inspected for food safety, reporters at WBEZ and the Sun Times:<br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-70d793c2-d4c8-11f1-9828-158d618d0b4b"><li>Obtained thousands of pages of records via the Freedom of Information Act from both the Chicago Department of Public Health, as well as the Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events, of on-the-ground health inspections at Taste and application materials from vendors.</li><li>Read and transcribed each page of the handwritten, scanned paper inspection forms from Taste of Chicago into a database, which was then vetted and fact-checked for accuracy, logging more than 1,000 inspections at the festival.</li><li>Identified the unique brick-and-mortar locations of each vendor, confirming addresses and business licenses on file within city databases, and contacting vendors with any discrepancies.</li><li>Compared each vendor’s brick-and-mortar health inspection records and application materials with the requirements set by the city for Taste of Chicago, and identified vendors with outdated or noncompliant health inspection records.</li><li>Contacted vendors who had notable inspection findings, and communicated our findings to the different city agencies that work to produce Taste of Chicago.</li></ul></div> </div><p>Asked about the Taste of Chicago inspection report, Richard Little, manager of the Chatham Oooh We! It Is!, said DCASE provides vendors with a trailer for vendors to store cold items. The trailers are shared by at least seven to 10 different businesses, he said, and on day one, the trailer was malfunctioning, through no fault of the restaurant’s own, Little said.“We never even got compensated for it,” Little said. He said he’d been in contact with someone from DCASE about receiving a dollar amount reimbursement for the malfunctioning trailer, but nobody from the department ever followed up with the restaurant, he said.</p><p>On day four of the festival, an inspector cited Oooh Wee for chopping green tomatoes on-site. Little told a reporter he received mixed messages about food preparation from the inspectors: One of them told him the tomatoes were fine to be chopped at the tent, while a second inspector hours later told them it was not allowed.“We like the Taste of Chicago, we appreciate the opportunity to be a part of it,” Little said. “Could things have been run a little bit smoother in regards to the inspection process and the malfunctioning of the refrigeration unit? I think they could have dealt with that a little better.”</p><p>Little said businesses like Oooh Wee spend so much time, resources and money to participate in events like the Taste of Chicago. “The general public and customers are most important. If [inspectors] say something needs to be thrown out ... we don't want to take any chances," he said.</p><p>Asked about malfunctioning trailers, DCASE said it contracted with an external company to provide the trailers, and there were no reports of them malfunctioning.</p><p>An analysis of records by WBEZ/Sun-Times reporters show the most common issue flagged by vendors at Taste was improper hot and cold holding temperatures for foods.</p><p>Inspectors, for example, discovered pre-cooked chicken held at improper temperatures at a Harold’s Chicken food truck on the first day of the festival, leading to employees discarding about 210 pounds of food.</p><p>At least 40 other vendors were cited for the issue by city inspectors, which led to at least 800 pounds of food being discarded throughout the festival.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-750000" eat.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Through CDPH, the City continues to prioritize strengthening food safety inspections, enforcement, and compliance efforts,” read a statement from a mayor’s office spokesperson. That includes multi-agency collaboration, preventative public messaging and staying “in touch with individuals testing positive for infections such as Cyclospora, tracing their food history to identify potential clusters,” the statement read.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-de0000" name="html-embed-module-de0000"></a><div style="min-height:728px" id="datawrapper-vis-3eNLO"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3eNLO/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-3eNLO"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3eNLO/full.png" alt="More than half of vendors at Taste of Chicago had health code violations (Table)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Private events overlooked </b></h3><p>Chicago street and neighborhood fests are usually brimming with food vendors, but according to a list of events inspected by CDPH and obtained by WBEZ/Sun-Times reporters, not all festivals are inspected every year. For example, Windy City Margarita Fest, which takes place in Pilsen each summer, was inspected this year but not in 2025.</p><p>City-sponsored events inspected by the department in 2026 include RibFest Chicago, Square Roots Festival and Market Days.“We prioritize events with higher numbers of vendors, so a lot of the street fests,” said Jacob Martin, the information coordinator for CDPH.</p><p>He said CDPH’s sanitarians do not inspect private events like Lollapalooza and Riot Fest even though they take place on public property. Lollapalooza <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2026/08/03/heres-what-grant-park-looks-like-after-lollapalooza-clears-the-stages" target="_blank" ><u>attracts more than 100,000 festivalgoers daily across four days</u></a> in Grant Park at the end of July, while Riot Fest brings an estimated 50,000 people a day to Douglass Park in September.</p><p>According to Martin, it is the job of CDPH to inspect a festival, but the department does not review or approve licenses or event requests. Public health sanitarians perform inspections at the request of a different city department, Business Affairs and Consumer Protection or BACP, which takes applications and approves license applications for events, such as the Taste of Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: ‘Looking for something different:’ Chicago Public Media launches online community
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Media, owner of the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ, soft-launched on Oct. 7 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/media/2026/07/08/chicago-public-media-launching-community-website-chicago-com-fall" target="_blank" ><u>chicago.com</u></a>, a new online platform focused on local communities.</p><p>The nonprofit rolled out its pilot in Chicago neighborhoods Avondale, Bronzeville, Edgewater/Andersonville and South Shore, as well as the city of Evanston.</p><p>Chicago.com expects to add more communities next spring or summer, said Melissa Bell, CEO of Chicago Public Media.</p><p>Each of the five Chicago.com communities has an events calendar, user-generated guides to local places, a forum where neighbors can share information and a weekly newsletter curated by a steward.</p><p>Chicago.com also curates headlines from the Sun-Times, WBEZ and other news sources.</p><p>Ahead of the launch, more than 4,000 people joined waitlists for the first five communities, according to a news release. Chicago Public Media did not disclose how many users it has.</p><p>A paid local resident moderates each community forum, and Chicago Public Media plans to hire a permanent general manager for Chicago.com.</p><p>The platform aims to be an alternative to for-profit social media platforms and to support non-toxic environments for civic discourse, Bell said.</p><p>So far, people are “really responding to the fact that this is human-led and very much an alternative to some of the faceless, nameless technology platforms that currently exist,” Bell said “People are interested in seeing an alternative on the marketplace that currently doesn't exist outside of the traditional Facebooks and Nextdoors.”</p><p>Chicago.com launched the pilot with tech nonprofit<b> </b>New_Public.</p><p>The Chicago Community Trust, a community foundation, owned the inactive chicago.com domain and gifted it to Chicago Public Media. The trust didn’t disclose the value of its in-kind gift.</p><p>Bell said Chicago Public Media has a budget for investing in Chicago.com but did not disclose how much.</p><p>The nonprofit is also still fundraising. “We're hoping to have the ability to have a bigger investment to move faster and ensure that we are building the product out as quickly as possible,” she said.</p><p>Bell added, “We had a very, very strong year last year, and we are able to actually ensure that we can reinvest into our organization.”</p><p>Kathy Herwig, Chicago.com steward for Edgewater/Andersonville, said, “People are really just looking for ways to help one another.” Users are sharing information about events, tradespeople and restaurants or discussing questions about gardening and tenants’ issues, she said.</p><p>People are “proactively saying that they're looking forward to this new space and saying that they want to help build it, and they want to help build a space for healthy community dialogue,” Herwig said. They “are looking for something different than what they're finding in other places.”</p><p>Herwig is a co-moderator of Edgewater’s Facebook group, which has about 11,000 members.</p><p>Rashanah Baldwin, Chicago.com steward for South Shore, said people are also sharing volunteer opportunities and neighborhood news. For example, users discussed a recent article about a street named for the late <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/09/22/donda-west-way-south-shore-street-renaming" target="_blank" ><u>Donda West</u></a>, mother of hip-hop artist Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. Donda West lived in South Shore and was an English professor at Chicago State University.</p><p>“We want that healthy community engagement, not just missing dogs or stolen packages,” Baldwin said. Chicago.com users are “looking for something different. They realize it's not Facebook. There aren't advertisements or algorithms, they don't have to navigate that.”</p><p>Baldwin previously moderated Englewood Portal, an online forum for the South Side neighborhood. She is also a co-chair of Chicago Public Media’s Sounding Board.</p><p>“I'm just looking for the platform to become that space where that old-school engagement comes back,” she said. “Seeing residents already post about what they're doing, like a bike meetup, if anyone wants to join. I'm looking forward to more residents who don't know each other connect online and move it to offline.”</p><p>Baldwin plans to hold more in-person meetings in the neighborhood with stakeholders, such as the local chamber of commerce at venues like South Shore Public Library.</p><p>The chicago.com launch comes at a time when many news organizations are struggling financially. In July, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/media/2026/07/08/chicago-public-media-launching-community-website-chicago-com-fall" target="_blank" ><u>Bell</u></a> said 2026 financial projections indicate Chicago Public Media will be “close to break-even.”</p><p>Chicago Public Media, parent of WBEZ, in 2022 acquired the Sun-Times and converted it from for-profit to nonprofit status, through a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2022/1/31/22911173/chicago-public-media-sun-times-sale-wbez-parent-donations-donors-philanthropy" target="_blank" ><u>$61 million, five-year pledge</u></a> from philanthropists and foundations.</p><p>Last year, the Sun-Times culled <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2025/03/18/chicago-sun-times-lose-20-staff-buyout-offer" target="_blank" ><u>20% of its news staff</u></a> through buyouts. In 2024, Chicago Public Media had layoffs that largely affected WBEZ staff and programming.</p>

entries.title: Despite Trump's harsh rhetoric toward Chicago, he's held significant private investments in the region
entries.summary: <p>Critics of President Donald Trump say there’s too often filth in his rhetoric, whether on social media or otherwise.</p><p>Records show Trump has also invested money in a local governmental agency tasked with cleaning up filth — the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, which treats sewage and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/30/raw-sewage-chicago-river-deep-tunnel-storms-climate-change" >combats flooding</a> in much of the Chicago region.</p><p>Governed by an elected board and spanning Cook County, the agency borrows money through the bond market for capital improvements and sometimes to refinance existing debt.</p><p>Trump had money in two bond issues from the sanitary district in 2025, according to economic disclosure statements released this summer that show one of the investments was valued at between $500,001 and $1 million, while the other was between $1,000,001 and $5 million.</p><p>There are few other details provided in the disclosure statements, except there’s a 5% interest rate on both bonds, one maturing in 2028 and the other in 2032.</p><p>There are several different MRWD bonds maturing in each of those years, and the disclosure records don’t make clear which series Trump is invested in.</p><p>But this much is known: Four bonds are coming due in 2028 ranging from $880,000 to $6.9 million in borrowing, officials said. There are three bonds maturing in 2032 ranging from $10 million to more than $48 million.</p><p>Neither the White House nor Trump’s business entity, the Trump Organization, would comment. But Trump and his aides have said that any trading in securities is done by third-party institutions to avoid any potential for a conflict of interest.</p><p>A spokesman for the reclamation district said recently: “We just got our credit ratings, and they look strong, and I think that speaks to our stable condition.”</p><p>“As to who invests in them, we’d have no clue.”</p><p>The agency’s board includes nine elected members, all Democrats, though several Republicans are running for seats in the upcoming general election. Reformers have asked throughout the years why a separate agency is needed at all for this kind of work, especially one overseen by a large elected body — whose bureaucracy also includes its own police force.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a20000" name="image-a20000"></a> <picture entries.title: Chicago to host an indie 'Cinema Weekend' celebrating local art house venues and filmmakers
entries.summary: <p>Chicago will host its first-ever "Cinema Weekend" celebrating independent and local film and the art house venues that screen such movies, organizers announced Monday. </p><p>The Chicago Film Office and <a class="Link" href="http://chicagoscrens.org" target="_blank" ><u>chicagoscreens.org</u></a> will host the inaugural <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoscreens.org/Chicago-Cinema-Weekend" target="_blank" >Chicago Cinema Weekend</a> from March 19-21. It will feature special programming, giveaways and screenings of films, from independent new releases to “Chicago-made classics.” </p><p>Some movies will be presented for free. Participating venues include the Music Box Theatre, the Gene Siskel Film Center, Facets Film Forum and the Claudia Cassidy Theater at the Chicago Cultural Center.</p><p>Popular pictures from the film festival season will also be presented by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/15/chicago-international-film-festival-celebrity-movie-red-carpet-john-c-reilly-derrick-rose" >Chicago International Film Festival</a>, Reeling: The Chicago LGBTQ+ International Film Festival, and the One Earth Film Festival.</p><p>Bucking a trend of declining audiences, independent film venues are drawing larger crowds following the COVID-19 pandemic. A 2025 <a class="Link" href="https://static1.squarespace.com/static/65c7b1d06ab3f94fdef53bf1/t/6a43fb7de8c0741476a3b739/1782840222985/AHC+2026+National+Audience+Survey+Report.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>survey</u></a> by the Art House Convergence nonprofit found that 25% of respondents began attending an independent cinema in the past three years. </p><p>A similar trend has been reported locally, according to the Chicago Alliance of Film Festivals, which operates <a class="Link" href="http://chicagoscreens.org" target="_blank" ><u>chicagoscreens.org</u></a>. The group’s venue members, which include Music Box Theatre, Gene Siskel Film Center and Facets Film Forum, have reported a growth in tickets sold, ranging from 45% to 95%, from 2023 to 2025.</p><p>Chicago Cinema Weekend aims to establish the city as a model for collaborative independent film programming.</p><p>“The Chicago audience has been growing like wildfire,” said Karen Cardarelli, the event’s executive producer and former executive director of Facets Film Forum. “They want a community experience. They want a cultural hub.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cc0000" with a community,” she said.</p><p>More participants will be added to the event over the coming months, and further details about programming will be announced early next year.</p><p>Across the arts entries.title: Man, 19, dies after Grand Boulevard Halloween shooting that wounded boy, 15
entries.summary: <p>A 19-year-old man who was shot and critically hurt along with a 15-year-old boy in the predawn hours of Halloween in the Grand Boulevard neighborhood has died. </p><p>Joseph Jackson, 19, and a 15-year-old boy were in the 500 block of East 50th Place around 12:25 a.m. when they were both shot, Chicago police said. </p><p>Wentworth District police officers responded to a person shot and found Jackson in the driver's seat of a black Chevrolet sedan with its driver's side windows shattered, suffering from multiple gunshot wounds to the head, according to a police report. </p><p>A short time later the teen was found shot in an apartment the 5000 block of South Washington Park Court. </p><p>Jackson, of Auburn Gresham, was shot in the head and taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office and police.</p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

Chicago, 81 vendors served up regional and international dishes to thousands of people across five days. The city's health inspectors logged more than 160 health code violations by those vendors during the festival, according to city records obtained by WBEZ and the Sun-Times. More than 70% of the fest's listed participants received violations, our analysis shows.</p><p><b>What was found</b>: Overflowing garbage. Backed-up sinks. Food prepped in bushes. entries.title: CEO of violence prevention group fatally gunned down in Chicago Heights office
entries.summary: <p>Someone fatally shot the CEO of a violence prevention group who worked in violence-plagued areas of Chicago on Saturday night in suburban Chicago Heights, officials said. </p><p>Andre Thomas, 57, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in the 400 block of West 14th Street around 9:25 p.m. Saturday, Chicago Heights police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Thomas was taken to an area hospital where he died of multiple gunshot wounds, according to the medical examiner's office, which ruled his death a homicide. </p><p>Thomas was the CEO and Executive Director of Integrity & Fidelity and was shot at his office, according to a statement from Chicago's 17th Ward Ald. David Moore. </p><p>"This is an unimaginable loss, not only for his family, friends, and colleagues, but also for the countless individuals and communities whose lives he touched through his leadership, commitment, and service," Moore wrote on Facebook. "My heart is heavy as I struggle to process this senseless act of violence."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Sun-Times expands Super 25: Every high school in Illinois eligible for football, basketball rankings
entries.summary: <p>The actual, physical newspaper was a vital part of my life for as long as I can remember. Chicago newspapers arrived in the morning, and the Joliet Herald-News arrived in the afternoon.</p><p>My mother read them every morning, and I followed suit as soon as I could. My first newspaper-related goal was to become the neighborhood paper boy. As with everything in the newspaper industry, getting that job was not straightforward. It required several years of buddying up to the older kid who held the gig. I filled in for him whenever he couldn’t work and helped on busy days with extra advertising flyers. When he finally turned 16 and moved on to a better-paying job, that canvas Herald-News bag was mine.</p><p>It took many more years (of similar politicking and underpaid work) to become the boys' basketball beat reporter at the Sun-Times and get the honor of selecting the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/11/01/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >Super 25 rankings</a>. For me, it is an honor, not just a job. The Sun-Times has nearly 80 years of history covering high school sports. It’s fulfilling to know that your work matters to people, and my email inbox after the rankings are released proves that every week.</p><p>When I sit down on Sunday morning to begin work on the football or basketball Super 25, it’s extremely serious and important to me—every decision matters. High school sports fans can sniff out a fraud. For the past 25 years, I’ve spent my falls and winters driving all over the area to see as many teams as possible so my opinions are informed, not wild guesses.</p><p>For the entire history of the Sun-Times, the Super 25 rankings consisted of teams in the print newspaper coverage area. That means places where the physical paper can be delivered. These days, that roughly means west to Plano, south to Kankakee, and north to the state line.</p><p>But the print newspaper isn’t what matters anymore, and it hasn’t been for a while. The Super 25 reaches readers all over the state on the website. Nearly every week, a reader in East St. Louis, Peoria, or another Illinois city reaches out and asks why their high school isn’t included in the Super 25.</p><p>That’s been on my mind for several years. After talking with Chris De Luca, the Sun-Times Sports Editor, we’ve decided to open up the Super 25 to the entire state. All 802 high schools in Illinois are now eligible for the Sun-Times’ new statewide Super 25 rankings. That’s double the number of schools currently in the Sun-Times’ print coverage area.</p><p>The change will begin this basketball season. Respected industry veteran Mike Clark will handle our girls basketball rankings this season, and I’ll do the boys rankings once again.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div I’ll be traveling outside of the Chicago area to cover some games this season, but luckily most of the top basketball teams from around the state regularly play games in the Chicago area these days.</p><p>Please be patient as we work things out. This will be a learning experience.</p><p>I’ve been watching high school basketball in Chicago since I was 13 years old and understand the rivalries and traditions. I’ve covered central and southern Illinois teams at the state finals and the Pontiac Holiday Tournament for decades. Still, I don't have deep knowledge of the Big Twelve or the Southwestern Conference. But I’m excited to learn and look forward to new (to me) gyms and all the new coaches, fans, and players I'll meet across the state.</p><p>Coaches, please email me your team information. Fans, keep me updated and tell me what games I should cover. I appreciate all the feedback. And always reach out when I have a ranking dead wrong.</p><p>Thanks for reading.</p>

entries.title: FOTOS: La Villita celebra el Día de Muertos
entries.summary: <p>La Calle 26 de La Villita se transformó en una gran celebración del Día de Muertos el domingo.</p><p>La festividad es una tradición anual el 1 y 2 de noviembre en México y en países de Centroamérica y Latinoamérica para honrar y celebrar a los seres queridos que han fallecido. La gente decora ofrendas o crea altares con cempasúchiles, calaveras de azúcar y fotos de sus seres queridos.</p><p>El sábado y el domingo, decenas de negocios de La Villita —incluyendo panaderías, taquerías, florerías, boutiques, bancos y espacios culturales— se sumaron a la celebración organizada por la Cámara de Comercio de La Villita. Los negocios participantes hicieron ofrendas y el personal se disfrazó de catrines y catrinas.</p><p>Ve las imágenes de las festividades:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Demolition has begun on Gary's storied Genesis Convention Center
entries.summary: <p>The Genesis Convention Center was supposed to symbolize the rebirth of Gary, Indiana, our famously beleaguered steel town neighbor to the east.</p><p>And it worked for a while. Built in 1981, the downtown building was the place for indoor sports, pageants and civic events. </p><p>The big hall, at 1 Genesis Center Plaza, once drew acts like Public Enemy, Whitney Houston, George Clinton, the Whispers and even Prince in a you-had-to-be-there 1982 concert with his protégés The Time and Vanity 6.</p><p>But the show is over now. </p><p>Closed since 2020, demolition crews are now ripping down the venue in the opening move of a major downtown <a class="Link" href="https://www.gary.gov/news-updates/city-of-gary-accelerates-downtown-development-with-multi-site-demolition-plan" target="_blank" >redevelopment effort</a>.</p><p>The city and the Northwest Indiana Regional Development Authority are also lowering the curtain on the nearby former H. Gordon & Sons department store. And there's more demolition to come.</p><p>"I don’t want our community to only see what is coming down, I want you to see what is coming next," Gary Mayor Eddie Melton said in a statement. "Holding on to unsalvageable buildings has cost our taxpayers millions and stalled our progress."</p><p>There's no question that Gary is long overdue for a rebirth, and keeping around vacant buildings that no one wants stands in the way of that.</p><p>Still, I hate to see the Genesis go. At least not without a few words about its passing.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The demolition continues at the Genesis Convention Center in Gary, Indiana.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Genesis was designed by Chicago architect Wendell Campbell and built by Gary's former Mayor Richard Hatcher, who first publicly talked about the need for a convention center in 1973.</p><p>Gary was a city of 175,000 in 1973 — it's about 70,000 now — and surrounding Lake County had a population of 545,000. Located near interstate expressways, rail and in close proximity to Chicago, a convention and entertainment center made sense.</p><p>Besides, Gary and its downtown were being threatened by white and middle-class flight and the near-demise of the steel industry. Something had to be done.</p><p>The 83,000-square-foot building had a 24,000-square-foot multipurpose arena that seated 7,000. There were meeting spaces and a ballroom that held 1,200.</p><p>Campbell's spaceship-like design of curves, right angles and projecting forms was clad in steel, the town's signature product. It looked futuristic and a bit quirky. And it was given a name that symbolized a new beginning.</p><p>Peabo Bryson performed there in 1982. Tickets were $12.50. A young Michael Jordan played the Bulls preseason games there in the 1980s. </p><p>Former President Barack Obama spoke to 7,000 Democratic Party voters there in a November 2018 <a class="Link" href="https://www.indystar.com/story/news/politics/2018/11/04/indiana-senate-race-obama-campaigns-donnelly-and-offers-antidote-trump/1858916002/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=true&gca-epti=z113628e008600v113628b0041xxd004165&gca-ft=122&gca-ds=sophi" target="_blank" ><u>get-out-the-vote rally</u></a>.</p><p>Hatcher’s December 2019 funeral turned out to be one of the Genesis' last major events before closing.</p><p>The city said the center "ran deep deficits for years, recouping only 33 cents for every dollar spent and costing taxpayers $8 million in operational shortfalls over five years alone."</p><p>Stabilizing and repairing the center would cost "in excess of $10 million," the city said.</p><p>The old Gordon's department store, at 801 Broadway, is being wrecked because it's an "imminent public hazard," according to the city. </p><p>The building has failing masonry, collapsed roof sections and damage caused by years of stormwater knifing through the structure.</p><p>Still, it's terrible that the exteriors of the four-story Prairie School building by the top-tier Chicago architect George W. Maher won't be saved and reused, especially with redevelopment dollars being pointed at the site. </p><p>Lauren Pacheco, a Gary artist and curator who is among a group of residents and activists whose mandate includes working to preserve the city's historic architecture, said she has "complicated feelings" about the Genesis' demolition.</p><p>"I also recognize the need for progress while acknowledging the loss of an important piece of Gary’s architectural and cultural history," she said. "Gary has spent decades being defined by what it’s lost. I’d love to see us shift that narrative toward what we have, what we’ve contributed and what we can imagine next."</p><p>And what comes next for the cleared sites?</p><p>The city and the redevelopment authority want to build a "modern municipal safety headquarters" — that means a police station; 150 residential units with ground-floor retail, a mini-grocer, restaurants at 5th and Broadway and 90 residences at 504 Broadway.</p><p>Also planned is a public space between the Lake County Courthouse, 400 Broadway, and the Hudson-Campbell Sports and Fitness Center, 455 Massachusetts St., that will commemorate the Genesis Center.</p><p>The city says its developing the plan with University of Notre Dame School of Architecture.</p><p>In a second phase, officials want to point the wrecking ball at the abandoned <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/09/05/city-methodist-church-largest-midwest-gary-demolition" >City Methodist Church</a>, at 577 Washington St., and the disused St. Mary’s Mercy Hospital, 540 Tyler St.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>City Methodist, a beauty that almost looks like Rockefeller Chapel gone to seed, closed in 1975 and has been a popular site for fashion photographers and urban explorers for years.</p><p>Michael Jackson was born at St. Mary's in 1958. The complex has been shuttered since 1995.</p><p>"We honor our history, and the generations of memories made here, but real revitalization requires courage and decisive action," Melton said of the redevelopment plan.</p><p>All this demolition. But the tabula rasa only goes so far. A solid preservation plan ought to ride along side this effort because there is still some good vintage architecture in Gary's downtown.</p><p>"I’m hopeful about Gary’s future, but I also believe that the most meaningful revitalization doesn’t erase a city’s identity," Pacheco said. "It builds upon it."</p>

entries.title: Ex-Chicago FBI boss sues Trump admin saying he was wrongly blamed for botched 'Broadview 6' case
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s former FBI boss sued top Trump administration officials Monday alleging that he resigned under duress after Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros sought to blame him for the implosion of the politically charged "Broadview Six" case.</p><p>Douglas DePodesta's lawsuit marks another extraordinary development in the tainted case against a group of Operation Midway Blitz protesters that has created a monthslong credibility crisis for Boutros. </p><p>In the lawsuit, filed in the Northern District of Illinois overseen by Boutros, DePodesta says President Donald Trump and other officials in Washington called for charges against those protesting the Midway Blitz deportation campaign last fall in the Chicago area. </p><p>In turn, Boutros brought "politically motivated prosecutions" that "were an unprecedented disaster" for his office, the lawsuit says. Boutros has adamantly denied that politics played any role in charging decisions.</p><p>When charges were dropped against the "Broadview Six" amid revelations of apparent prosecutorial misconduct, "Boutros began a campaign within the Department of Justice to blame DePodesta for the unraveling of the case." Boutros' complaints to superiors in Washington ultimately led to DePodesta's ouster, the lawsuit says.</p><p>The FBI, the Justice Department, Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel are targeted as defendants in the lawsuit alongside Boutros, who is named in his personal and professional capacities.</p><p>“The American people need to know what is happening within their government,” DePodesta, Chicago’s former<b> </b>FBI<b> </b>special-agent-in-charge,<b> </b>told the Sun-Times in an interview.</p><p>DePodesta acknowledged the lawsuit will likely put a target on his back. But, he insisted, “I will not let fear silence me.”</p><p>“I was forced to leave my job,” DePodesta said. “I was ordered to leave my job.”</p><p>DePodesta filed his lawsuit four months after news broke of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/01/chicago-fbi-chief-depodesta-leaving-unexpectedly-ongoing-credibility-crisis-federal-prosecutors-us-attorney" >his sudden, unexpected departure</a> from the FBI. It came weeks after the “Broadview Six” scandal rocked the Dirksen Federal Courthouse. </p><p>The news opens a new legal front in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >the “Broadview Six” scandal</a>, which Friday<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/30/controversial-doj-boss-takes-reins-in-tainted-broadview-6-case-stymies-judges-inquiry" >drew in the Justice Department’s third-highest ranking official</a>, Stanley Woodward. He has increasingly found himself at the center of the Justice Department's national controversies, including the East Potomac Golf Course and the Alaska Senate race.</p><p>DePodesta’s lawsuit also points to a potential rift in Chicago’s federal law enforcement community, which has long touted the value of partnerships.</p><p>Boutros and DePodesta shared credit for the filing of high-profile criminal charges as recently as early July. Boutros is considered the region’s top federal law enforcement official, and DePodesta led one of the Justice Department's most prominent agencies here.</p><p>Now they’re legal adversaries, in a lawsuit sure to get national attention. The lawsuit seeks DePodesta’s reinstatement, back pay, compensatory damages and attorneys’ fees. He also wants declarations that the defendants violated his rights and the procedures for terminating an employee.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"
