class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>If a judge lets DePodesta’s lawsuit move forward, it could also lead to new revelations about what went on behind the scenes during the doomed “Broadview Six” prosecution. DePodesta's lawsuit has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly.</p><p>It all comes as controversy continues to swirl around the Justice Department. DePodesta’s attorney, former federal prosecutor Ron<b> </b>Safer, also represents Bradley<b> </b>Benavides, one of two former<b> </b>FBI officials<b> </b>charged<b> </b>last month with making false statements to Congress. A federal magistrate judge threw out the charges against them<b> </b>Monday, calling it a political prosecution, according to news reports.</p><p>DePodesta, a 24-year FBI veteran, recently<b> </b>spoke with the Sun-Times<b> </b>about the end of his law enforcement career and how he views the role of the FBI — under any presidential administration.</p><p>DePodesta led<b> </b>the FBI’s Chicago Field Office<b> </b>for nearly two years, starting in August 2024. He left July 6, six weeks after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" >the “Broadview Six” case collapsed</a> in spectacular fashion. Boutros wound up facing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/05/boutros-broadview-six-perry" >a credibility crisis</a>, with judges questioning whether they could trust his team.</p><p>Even now, U.S. District Judge April Perry<b> </b>is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/01/broadview-six-perry-boutros-mecklenburg" >considering whether to appoint<b> </b>a special prosecutor</a><b> </b>to investigate Boutros and others<b> </b>for criminal contempt. She<b> </b>recently<b> </b>asked a lawyer<b> </b>from Boutros’ office whether any member of his team would invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination<b> </b>— and he didn’t rule it out.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” case revolved around <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" >a protest outside an immigration holding facility</a> in west suburban Broadview<b> </b>in September 2025, at the height of Operation Midway Blitz. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV.</p><p>But from that crowd, only six people were charged with<b> </b>conspiring<b> </b>to impede<b> </b>the agent, a felony carrying a maximum six-year prison sentence. Most of the defendants were involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about selective prosecution.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5b0000" name="image-5b0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/899076a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/359e441/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/98b90b5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The so-called "Broadview Six." Clockwise from top left: Michael Rabbitt, Brian Straw, Kat Abughazaleh, Andre Martin, Joselyn Walsh and Catherine “Cat” Sharp." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/98b90b5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/753aa7f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/98b90b5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A composite of photos of the so-called “Broadview Six.” Clockwise from top left: Michael Rabbitt, Brian Straw, Kat Abughazaleh, Andre Martin, Joselyn Walsh and Catherine<b> </b>“Cat”<b> </b>Sharp.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The case collapsed<b> </b>May 21 after Perry discovered alleged prosecutorial misconduct in grand jury transcripts<b> </b>that she said left her “incredibly shocked.”</p><p>The spotlight wound up on one prosecutor in particular, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/24/broadview-six-sheri-mecklenburg" >Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg</a>. But Boutros couldn’t shake questions about the role he and others played in the case. By the time of DePodesta’s unexpected departure, Boutros had already endured weeks of bad headlines.</p><p>DePodesta denied to the Sun-Times that he’d improperly put his thumb on the scale of any prosecution. He also dismissed the idea that family ties created any conflict of interest.</p><p>DePodesta’s<b> </b>sister-in-law<b> </b>is a defense attorney who represents Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt, one member of the “Broadview Six.”</p><p>She’s a former federal prosecutor who has gone on to represent individuals in other cases brought by the FBI, DePodesta pointed out.<b> </b>And it’s not unusual for attorneys — even judges — to have past associations with each other.</p><p>“There are lots of relationships like mine and hers within this community,” DePodesta said.</p><p>Meanwhile, DePodesta said the FBI in Chicago “did a very, very good job enforcing immigration law” in the second Trump administration. It did so, he said, “because it was lawful.”<b> </b>He said he even checked with the lawyers to make sure.</p><p>“When things are lawful, and it aligns with the administration’s strategy, 100% we’re on board,” DePodesta said.</p><p>“The issue,” he added, “is when it deviates from the law and the Constitution.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" stressed that “despite alternate rhetoric or branding tactics, the FBI’s mission remains unchanged: to uphold the U.S. Constitution and protect the American people.”</p><p>DePodesta said he learned through a phone call, “completely out of the blue,” that he’d need to leave his job in Chicago. The news came from a top official, he said.<b> </b>But the brass also made clear to him that the decision was “not performance-based.”</p><p>Still, DePodesta said, “it was horrible.”</p><p>“I described it before as a little like a death, really,” DePodesta told the Sun-Times.<b> </b>“It was a part of me. … My profession was who I was.”</p><p>DePodesta said he is now the director of business development for a startup company. But he said he’s also applied for security jobs, and has “had a very hard time getting employment.”</p><p>“One could reasonably believe there was a reason for that, right?” DePodesta said. “Because of the way I was publicly removed.”</p><p>He didn’t rule out returning to law enforcement one day. He acknowledged his lawsuit will bring him back into the spotlight. But, he said, “I feel so strongly about letting people know what happened.”</p><p>“I hope others speak up about what is happening within this government,”<b> </b>DePodesta said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/01/chicago-fbi-chief-depodesta-leaving-unexpectedly-ongoing-credibility-crisis-federal-prosecutors-us-attorney" >Chicago FBI chief leaving unexpectedly, raising eyebrows amid feds’ ongoing credibility crisis</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/02/chicago-fbi-chief-departure-depodesta-message-to-staff-us-attorney-boutros-trump" >Outgoing Chicago FBI chief tells team to ‘keep the FBI mission alive’ as speculation swirls about his exit</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Review: ‘The Royale’ at Writers Theatre
entries.summary: <p>Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became the first Black man to win boxing’s heavyweight championship, is buried at Graceland Cemetery in Uptown. In a place known for elaborate shrines to the city’s most famous, his grave went for six decades without any individual marker at all, only a single tombstone for his family’s plot reading, simply, “Johnson.” Following the 2005 release of Ken Burns’ documentary about him, “Unforgivable Blackness,” a small flat stone was placed to single him out and note his historic achievement.</p><p>The modesty of his burial site doesn’t reflect the man’s personality. Johnson was full of swagger and fond of fast cars and furs. His biggest victories against white champions, when finally allowed, were followed by violent riots. There’s something about the bareness of the sport of boxing that made its champion an emblem of raw physical superiority, and therefore made the ring an arena in which racial identity felt raw and significant.</p><p>The tension between the ambition of excellence and fear of the consequences surrounding African-American accomplishment becomes the core theme of Marco Ramirez’s play “The Royale,” inspired by Johnson’s ascent to the boxing crown and receiving an elegant, beautifully acted revival at Writers Theatre under the direction of Definition Theatre’s founder Tyrone Phillips.</p><div Through Nov. 29<br><b>Where:</b> Writers Theatre, 325 Tudor Court, Glencoe<br><b>Tickets:</b> $35-$100<br><b>Info:</b> writerstheatre.org<br><b>Run time:</b> 85 minutes, no intermission</div> </div><p>“The Royale” was first produced in 2013, revised for its Chicago debut in 2015, and went on to well-received productions off-Broadway and on regional stages for years.</p><p>The play’s popularity stems from its core theatrical conceit, which works exceptionally well here. The fights are represented without physical contact, with stomping and clapping to represent the blows (the movement direction is from Rasell Holt). The rhythmic percussion — without the help of any instruments — extends to other scenes as well, providing a stylized sensibility that fits with its highly condensed, focused storytelling.</p><p>This is a bio-play that homes in on its theme without concern for everything it leaves out or fictionalizes for efficiency. Everything here is minimal, as boxing matches tend to be. Lauren M. Nichols’ set is little more than wood planks, a brick background and a punching bag or microphone. The boxing scenes barely require any clothing, although costume designer Gregory Graham provides period-specific garb elsewhere that tells quite a bit about differences in characters’ class status, or at least their aspirations to it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b80000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Hugo Hentoff</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>During the matches, Jason Lynch’s lighting plays a significant role, emphasizing how alone a boxer is, no matter how much the endeavor may represent something bigger.</p><p>The five-person cast here is excellent. La’Tevin Alexander plays Johnson’s stand-in, here named Jay Jackson, not just with plenty of physical power but with a strong sense of destiny. He’s particularly able to make us curious why his character refuses to talk about his past, and then to dig deeper when he is finally forced to, upon the arrival of his sister Nina. Nina is the cautious one, and in AnJi White’s performance at first hesitant and then eager to voice everything bad that could happen if Jay were to win the “Fight of the Century,” and certainly not just to Jay himself.</p><p>The supporting characters here tend to be functional but each actor has their moments. James Vincent Meredith delivers a soulful, easygoing-yet-wise take on Jay’s coach; Ajax Dontavius brings an important likability to the younger rival-turned-sparring partner Fish; and Scott Aiello plays the white promoter Max without resorting to stereotype, even when he tries to explain dynamics that Jay is always fully aware of.</p><p>Could the production be even more atmospheric, more musical, more choreographic? Probably. But I think Phillips here is looking to emphasize the contemplative nature of Ramirez’s play, which continues to reflect so much on society.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Key education endorsements for CPS School Board candidates
entries.summary: <p>As part of our<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" > voter guide</a>, we assembled a list of organizations involved in education-related work that have made endorsements in the 2026 Chicago School Board election. We are also listing education-focused political action committees that don’t endorse but are providing financial support to specific candidates.</p><p>We are not listing all endorsements, including from elected officials, non-education organizations or those that aren’t directly tied to Chicago Public Schools. Those are available on each candidate’s website.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Teachers Union</u></b></a>: The largest union in CPS, including nearly 30,000 teachers, paraprofessionals, clinicians and school-related personnel, known for its strong focus on social justice issues.</p><p><b>Chicago Democrats for Education</b>: This political action committee was launched during the first school board election in 2024 to support “independent” candidates for the school board. The group was set up to be a counterbalance to the CTU and the mayor. It was formed by Hugo Jacobo, a heavyweight political consultant.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.theschoolleader.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Principals & Administrators Association</u></b></a>: This union represents CPS principals, assistant principals and other districtwide and central office administrators.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://cgcollective.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Common Ground Collective</u></b></a>: A new political action committee that is anti-CTU, heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.” The group says it wants to “defeat extremist efforts from both the far right and far left that seek to divide our city.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://incsaction.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>INCS Action PAC</u></b></a><b> for Public Charter Schools</b>: This political action committee is affiliated with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, which advocates on behalf of publicly funded, independently run charter schools. It is “focused on engaging the charter school community in the legislative and political process.” The group hasn’t made endorsements as of mid-September, but has donated to select candidates.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://wearelee.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Leadership for Educational Equity</u></b></a><b>, LEE PAC:</b> This group also donates under the name Leaders in Education. This organization and affiliated political action committee provides support and campaign services for reduced costs for alumni of education nonprofit groups, including Teach for America, New Leaders and School Board Partners, and other civic-minded organizations. The other civic-minded organizations include the Academy for Local Leadership Chicago, which offers training for education advocates and aspiring school board members. Alumni of a year-long ALL fellowship include Brenda Lee Anderson, Carlos Rivas Jr. and Jesus Ayala Jr. Therese Boyle also participates in ongoing training offered by ALL.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://onepeoplescampaign.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>ONE People’s Campaign</u></b></a><b>:</b> This grassroots campaign says it puts “the interests of regular people before the profits of corporations and the super rich” and focuses on supporting and endorsing progressive causes.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://publicschoolchampions.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Our Schools Chicago</u></b></a><b>: </b>A CTU-affiliated group with a platform that mirrors the one advanced by Hilario Dominguez, the CTU-endorsed candidate for school board president. entries.title: Former FBI boss' lawsuit undermines Boutros' denial of Washington's role in 'Broadview 6' case
entries.summary: <p>The lawsuit brought Monday<b> </b>by Chicago’s former FBI boss undercuts a key claim made by U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office about the politically charged “Broadview Six” case — one that a judge had already sought to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/09/feds-appear-to-hide-name-of-government-lawyer-in-new-broadview-six-court-filing" target="_blank" >put under a microscope</a>.</p><p>Boutros’ office<b> </b>told<b> </b>U.S. District Judge April Perry<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/30/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >in March</a><b> </b>that there were “no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone outside [the U.S. attorney’s office] (other than the local FBI investigators assigned to the case) regarding any investigatory or charging decisions.</p><p>“To be crystal clear, this specifically includes anyone in the White House" or at Justice Department headquarters in Washington, prosecutors wrote<b> </b>March 30.</p><p>But Monday, former FBI Special Agent in Charge Douglas<b> </b>DePodesta<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/02/fbi-boutros-depodesta-broadview-six" target="_blank" >alleged in a lawsuit</a> that Boutros<b> </b>met<b> </b>in DePodesta’s office Oct. 7, 2025, with then-Deputy Attorney General Todd<b> </b>Blanche, FBI Director Kash<b> </b>Patel<b> </b>and<b> </b>Assistant Attorney General Colin<b> </b>McDonald.</p><p>“During this meeting, Defendant Boutros discussed the Broadview Six investigation with his superiors in the Department of Justice and other law enforcement officers,” DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the lawsuit.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a90000" “Broadview Six” case two days later, records show. They eventually secured it Oct. 23, 2025, after the case was initially rejected by a grand jury. </p><p>The charges, made public days later, drew swift criticism and raised questions about whether Boutros' office had targeted people for opposing the Trump administration. Meanwhile, defense attorneys have continued to press for information about any role the administration has played in the high-profile case.</p><p>DePodesta<b> </b>on<b> </b>Monday<b> </b>sued<b> </b>Boutros, Patel, Blanche, the FBI and the Justice Department, alleging<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>falsely blamed<b> </b>DePodesta<b> </b>for the collapse of the “Broadview Six” case. DePodesta alleged that Boutros’ campaign<b> </b>led to DePodesta’s forced<b> </b>retirement.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/02/fbi-boutros-depodesta-broadview-six" >Ex-Chicago FBI boss sues Trump administration, says he was wrongly blamed for botched ‘Broadview 6’ case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The lawsuit opens a new legal front in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six” scandal</a>, which<b> </b>Friday<b> </b>drew in the Justice Department’s third-highest ranking official, Stanley Woodward. Perry is also considering whether to name a special prosecutor to look into wrongdoing by the feds.</p><p>Neither Boutros nor a spokesperson immediately commented on the lawsuit Monday.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” case revolved around a protest outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV.</p><p>But from that crowd, only six people were charged with a conspiracy to impede the agent. Most of them were involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about selective prosecution.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-820000" name="image-820000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/899076a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/359e441/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/98b90b5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The so-called "Broadview Six." that “persons close to the Trump administration called for criminal prosecution of the protesters, particularly Kat Abughazaleh, who was running for the office of United States Representative at the time.”</p><p>Abughazaleh, a high-profile progressive<b> </b>known for her social media livestreams, wound up placing second in the crowded Democratic<b> </b>primary<b> </b>race<b> </b>for<b> </b>Illinois’<b> </b>9th<b> </b>District<b> </b>House<b> </b>seat. That race was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/us-house-illinois-9th-congressional-district-primary-results" target="_blank" >won by Daniel<b> </b>Biss</a>.</p><p>Boutros’ team<b> </b>later<b> </b>argued<b> </b>that<b> </b>claims<b> </b>of<b> </b>selective<b> </b>or<b> </b>vindictive<b> </b>prosecution<b> </b>were<b> </b>“the product of fevered paranoia and delusional speculation.”</p><p>The case <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >collapsed May 21</a>, after Perry discovered apparent misconduct by prosecutors before the grand jury.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/30/controversial-doj-boss-takes-reins-in-tainted-broadview-6-case-stymies-judges-inquiry" >Controversial DOJ boss takes reins in tainted ‘Broadview 6’ case, stymies judge’s inquiry</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Early last month, Perry<b> </b>asked<b> </b>Boutros’ office to turn over records related to key claims made by the feds. Woodward, the associate attorney general,<b> </b>asked her on Friday to clarify<b> </b>whether that “request”<b> </b>was really a “directive.”<b> </b>He<b> </b>also warned her that “the United States has not agreed to provide any information.”</p><p>One claim that’s drawn Perry’s interest is whether Boutros’ office communicated with anyone outside the office — including with White House or Justice Department officials — about the case. Despite the claim made by Boutros’ office in March, a lawyer from his office recently seemed to suggest such communications might exist, after all.</p><p>During an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/01/broadview-six-perry-boutros-mecklenburg" target="_blank" >Oct. 1 hearing</a>, Perry<b> </b>told<b> </b>Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathaniel<b> </b>Whalen<b> </b>she’d been told “there’s nothing. No way, no how.</p><p>“And now,” she said, “your argument has changed pretty significantly.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox claim infielder Graham Pauley off waivers, outright two others
entries.summary: <p>Monday’s deadline for MLB teams to cut down their 40-man rosters to their maximum size always prompts a little bit of player movement across the league. Despite reinstating all six players off their 60-day injured list on Thursday without issue, the White Sox were not sidelined.</p><p>The team announced they’ve claimed infielder Graham Pauley off waivers from the Marlins. A former 13th-round pick of the Padres who came to Miami as part of a package for closer Tanner Scott, Pauley is a career .209/.272/.364 hitter over parts of three major-league seasons. The 26-year-old has mostly played third base with the Marlins and rated well there defensively, and his tenure overlapped with that of hitting coach Sox Derek Shomon. He offers potential depth as a multi-position reserve, but is unlikely to man an up-the-middle position.</p><p>There is room for Pauley on the White Sox 40-man roster because they cleared off two spots on Monday as well. Outfielder Junior Perez and left-hander Ky Bush were both outrighted to Triple-A Charlotte, meaning they cleared waivers and will remain in the Sox organization.</p><p>Perez, 25, hit .171/.194/.429 in 22 games with the Sox after being acquired from the A’s for minor league pitcher Jackson Nove in May. The speedy outfielder is an impressive athlete with plus raw power, and launched his first major league homer off two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal in June. But his strikeout issues relegated him to part-time player status, and the acquisition of fellow right-hander centerfielder Brenton Doyle blocked Perez’s path to further playing time in Chicago.</p><p>Back in 2024, Bush was part of a dominant Double-A rotation that looked like a glimpse of the Sox rotation’s future. The mustachioed Utah left-handed made his big league debut at the tail-end of that season (5.60 ERA, 17 ⅔ IP) but was troubled by a triceps injury and physical ailments have wiped out his last two seasons. Bush underwent Tommy John surgery in spring of 2025, and his rehab process was stalled by a triceps strain this past year.</p><p>The activity has left the Sox 40-man roster with one open spot, but that’s surely underselling the level of turnover to come over the next month.</p>

entries.title: Early voting, mail ballot turnout in Cook County surpass 2022 levels by nearly 30%
entries.summary: <p>Early voting and mail-in ballot turnout in suburban Cook County for the midterm elections has surpassed turnout in the 2022 gubernatorial election by nearly 30% so far, Cook County Clerk Monica Gordon said Monday. </p><p>More than 242,000 residents have cast ballots during early voting as of Monday morning. Nearly 107,000 mail ballots have been returned and 11,000 are in the postal service pipeline.</p><p>Early voting turnout is expected to exceed 2022 levels by 50,000, and mail-in ballot turnout is also projected to surpass 2022 levels by the same margin, said Edmund Michalowski, deputy clerk of elections.</p><p>“Our priority has been to make voting as convenient and accessible as possible,” Gordon entries.title: East Aurora District 131 board member denies allegations of kickback scheme following federal charges
entries.summary: <p>An East Aurora School District member facing federal charges for an alleged kickback scheme has denied the allegations in her first public statement since the grand jury indictment dropped last week.</p><p>Annette Johnson, the former board president who signed the statement as a member of East Aurora School District 131, maintained her innocence and said she intended to “vigorously defend myself through the judicial process.”</p><p>“I recognize the gravity of these allegations, and I do not take the concerns of our residents, parents, or taxpayers lightly,” Johnson said in a statement Monday. “I take these allegations seriously, but I will not allow them to define me or erase the years of service and commitment I have devoted to this community.”</p><p>According to a grand jury indictment released last week, Johnson is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/27/east-aurora-district-131-board-member-facing-federal-charges-over-fraud-kickback-scheme" target="_blank" ><u>charged</u></a> with two counts of honest services mail fraud and one count of honest services wire fraud after allegedly using her position as board president to push the district to buy $2.7 million in wearable air purifiers in 2021 in exchange for a $1.3 million payment to a company that Johnson helped lead.</p><p>Johnson was allegedly paid $7,500 that year by a company involved in the dealing, though she didn’t list it on her statement of economic interest filed with Kane County, according to the indictment.</p><p>The next day, Aurora mayor John Laesch said a whistleblower approached him in 2024 to report that Johnson purportedly had ties to eight companies, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/10/29/aurora-john-laesch-annette-johnson-corruption" target="_blank" ><u>made $43.1 million from the school district between 2018 and 2023</u></a>, according to district records provided by Laesch. He called for Johnson's resignation in a statement released that day.</p><p>Johnson’s economic conflicts were left blank for 13 years, until 2025, when she listed the Elk Grove-based DJ Payne Corporation, according to filings with Kane County.</p><p>Months earlier, her candidacy was challenged by an Aurora resident who alleged she worked for DJ Payne and other companies, at least one of which did business with the school district when she was board president. The board dropped the issue after deciding it didn’t have the authority to challenge the validity of her economic statements.</p><p>In 2025, a year after the ruling, Johnson listed DJ Payne for the first time in her economic interest statement. The company’s website still lists Johnson as part of its sales team.</p><p>The school district said in a statement it was aware of the allegations and working with investigators, but wouldn't comment on her position on the board.</p><p>Johnson is set to serve on the board through April 2029, per the district’s website. She is due in court on the charges Nov. 9, according to court filings.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/10/29/aurora-john-laesch-annette-johnson-corruption" >$43M flowed from school district to firms linked to indicted board member, Aurora mayor says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/27/east-aurora-district-131-board-member-facing-federal-charges-over-fraud-kickback-scheme" >East Aurora District 131 board member facing federal charges over fraud, kickback scheme</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson forced to use $75M parking meter windfall to pay extra on pension debt
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Monday suffered the latest in a string of City Council defeats — a loss that blows a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/27/special-city-council-meeting-stonepeak-partners-chicago-parking-meters-deal-brandon-johnson-budget" >$75 million hole </a>in his preelection budget.</p><p>At a special meeting that the Johnson administration tried to avoid, a veto-proof City Council majority voted 44-6 to compel Johnson to apply the $75 million up-front payment from Stonepeak Partners, the New York investment firm that acquired Chicago's parking meters, to the 2026 city budget for use as an extra payment that chips away at the city’s $36 billion pension crisis.</p><p>Without consulting the Council, Johnson decided to use the $75 million windfall to help defray the cost of the $363 million pension advance for 2027. </p><p>The police and fire pension funds most in danger of insolvency — with assets to cover just 26.4% and 25.2% of liabilities respectively — will each receive $25.12 million “no later than Dec. 31.”</p><p>The Municipal Employees and Laborers pension funds — with unfunded ratios of 28.1% and 44.1% respectively — will each receive $12.375 million, the ordinance states.</p><p>Finance Chair and 3rd Ward Ald. Pat Dowell led the negotiating team that persuaded Stonepeak to pay the city $75 million up front, and 5% of profit-sharing going forward. Dowell estimated that Monday’s vote would “conservatively” save city employee pension funds “$213 million over time.”</p><p>“For too long, one-off revenues and asset leases have been used to fill immediate, short-term budget holes at the expense of our long-term financial health,” Dowell told her colleagues.</p><p>“We are drawing a hard line in the sand — not just for today but for the future of Chicago’s fiscal management. Securing our four pension funds is not just a statutory requirement. It is a moral obligation to the workforce that keeps this city moving. I urge my colleagues to stand on the right side of history, locking this into city code, securing this additional revenue for our pensions now and for the remaining 57 years of this contract.”</p><p>For those who are “worried about the hole” created by Monday’s vote, Dowell said, “I stand ready to work with my colleagues to vet and implement any proposal the mayor puts forth to adjust his budget in response.”</p><p>“When you have a lot of debt, sometimes you have to eat beans while you’re paying off the debt,” Dowell said. “We are doing just that." </p><p>Budget Chair and 28th Ward Ald. Jason Ervin, the mayor’s most powerful ally, tried and failed to shame his colleagues into backing off by pointing to the people programs that he said will now need to be sacrificed because of what he called the “overpayment” to city employee pension funds.</p><p>They include funding for tree-trimming, rodent control and other city housekeeping services, as well as for libraries, youth jobs, The group is calling for $75 million in Chicago parking meter funds to be used for libraries, youth jobs and city services instead of extra pension payments. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Vote your conscience, but understand that folks are gonna lose out in this for something that we are going to, theoretically, overpay on,” Ervin said. “I don’t know anybody [who] pays two years' rent ahead of time when we don’t have the basics in communities today. That is tantamount to what we’re doing.”</p><p>Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez (25th), who joined Ervin in casting one of the six “no” votes, said he was “sick and tired of coming into this chamber to decide what was already decided by the few.”</p><p>“In the budget hearings, I’ve been hearing how much we need more youth jobs. … How are we gonna pay for it?” Sigcho-Lopez asked.</p><p>After the vote, the mayor's office released a statement saying, "Directing these dollars toward an additional payment comes with a potential trade-off for Chicagoans, putting youth jobs, homelessness services, libraries, community violence intervention programs, and basic neighborhood services at risk. The Johnson administration will continue fighting to protect them and ensure our neighborhoods receive the resources they need and deserve.”</p><p>Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) rejected what he called the “false choice” between dire budget cuts and fiscal responsibility.</p><p>Monday’s vote marks the latest in a string of Council defeats for Johnson, who has struggled to pass his last two budgets, issued four mayoral vetoes, cast several tie-breaking votes and has been forced accept a Zoning Committee chair he did not choose.</p><p>Even more troubling for the mayor is the $75 million hole created by Monday’s vote that is almost certain to get bigger.</p><p>If 29 alderpersons make good on their threat to reject<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/20/mayor-brandon-johnson-failed-corporate-head-tax-resurrected-proposed-budget" > Johnson’s revived corporate head tax,</a> the budget gap will be $176 million. If they reject or reduce Johnson’s plan to raise the Chicago tax on equipment rentals and cloud computing to 20% or oppose his plan to borrow $480 million for police settlements, the gap could top $400 million.</p>
